1.summary: Skipping his usual thanksgiving, Paul is astonished that the Galatians are turning to a different gospel and pronounces a curse on anyone who preaches one; he recounts that he received his gospel by revelation from Jesus Christ, not from any human.
1.lookfor: Notice what is missing after the greeting, and Paul's emphasis on his independence from Jerusalem.

names.name: Galatia
names.gloss: A Roman province in central Asia Minor (modern Turkey).

names.name: Arabia
names.gloss: The Nabataean kingdom east and south of Damascus.

names.name: Damascus
names.gloss: The city where Paul met Jesus.

names.name: Peter
names.gloss: The apostle, also called Cephas, whom Paul visited for fifteen days.

names.name: James
names.gloss: The Lord's brother, leader in Jerusalem.

insights.title: No thanksgiving
insights.body: Every other letter of Paul's opens with thanks or praise for the readers. Here he goes straight to I marvel that you are so quickly deserting (1:6). The omission is a sign of alarm.

insights.title: Another gospel
insights.body: The rival teachers didn't deny Jesus; they added to him: believe in Christ, and also be circumcised. Paul says any addition makes it a different gospel, which is really no gospel at all (1:7).

insights.title: Accursed
insights.body: If anyone, even an angel, preaches another gospel, let him be anathema (1:8-9), devoted to destruction. Paul repeats it for emphasis.

insights.title: Not from man
insights.body: Paul received his gospel not from any person but through revelation of Jesus Christ (1:12). His critics claimed he got it second-hand and watered it down.

insights.title: Zealous for traditions
insights.body: Paul advanced in Judaism beyond many of his age, extremely zealous for the traditions of his fathers (1:14). Zeal was the word for violent defense of the law, like Phinehas.

insights.title: Set apart from the womb
insights.body: God set Paul apart from his mother's womb and called him by grace (1:15), echoing the calls of Jeremiah and Isaiah's servant.

insights.title: They glorified God
insights.body: The churches of Judea only heard that the former persecutor now preaches the faith he once tried to destroy, and they glorified God because of me (1:23-24).

insights.title: Pleasing people
insights.body: Paul asks whether he is trying to please people; if so, he wouldn't be Christ's servant (1:10). Whose approval drives you most?

2.summary: Paul tells how the Jerusalem leaders accepted his gospel without requiring Titus to be circumcised, and how he confronted Peter in Antioch for withdrawing from table fellowship with Gentiles; he declares that we are justified by faith in Christ, and that he lives by faith in the Son of God who loved him.
2.lookfor: Notice the handshake in Jerusalem, the clash in Antioch, and the personal confession at the end.

names.name: Barnabas
names.gloss: Paul's partner, who was carried away by the hypocrisy at Antioch.

names.name: Titus
names.gloss: A Greek believer brought to Jerusalem as a test case.

names.name: Antioch
names.gloss: Antioch in Syria, the mixed Jewish and Gentile church.

names.name: John
names.gloss: The apostle John, a pillar of the Jerusalem church.

insights.title: Titus not compelled
insights.body: Not even Titus, a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised (2:3). The Jerusalem leaders' acceptance of an uncircumcised believer settled the point in principle.

insights.title: The right hand of fellowship
insights.body: James, Cephas and John, reputed pillars, gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship (2:9). A handshake sealed agreements; it marked partnership, with Paul to the Gentiles and Peter to the circumcised.

insights.title: Remember the poor
insights.body: Their only request: remember the poor, which Paul was eager to do (2:10). The collection for Jerusalem fills his later letters.

insights.title: Confronting Peter
insights.body: In Antioch Peter ate with Gentiles until people came from James, then withdrew for fear of the circumcision party (2:12). Paul opposed him to his face, because separating tables denied that Gentiles were full members.

insights.title: Justified by faith
insights.body: A person is not justified by works of the law but by faith in Jesus Christ (2:16). Works of the law here especially means the markers that separated Jews from Gentiles: circumcision, food laws, festivals.

insights.title: Christ lives in me
insights.body: I have been crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me, by faith in the Son of God who loved me and gave himself for me (2:20). Doctrine becomes personal confession.

insights.title: Who loved me
insights.body: Paul says the Son of God loved me and gave himself for me. How would you live today if you believed that personally?

3.summary: Paul asks the Galatians whether they received the Spirit by works of the law or by faith, shows that Abraham was justified by faith and that Christ became a curse to redeem us from the law's curse, explains the law's temporary role, and declares that in Christ there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female.
3.lookfor: Notice the questions Paul fires at them, the law as a guardian, and the great statement of unity at the end.

names.name: Abraham
names.gloss: The father of all who believe, who trusted God's promise.

insights.title: Foolish Galatians
insights.body: O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you? (3:1). The word bewitched was used of the evil eye, a spell that fascinated a victim. Paul can't believe they've been charmed away.

insights.title: How you received the Spirit
insights.body: Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law or by hearing of faith? (3:2). Their own experience proves the point: God gave his Spirit to uncircumcised believers.

insights.title: All nations blessed
insights.body: Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced to Abraham: in you all the nations will be blessed (3:8). The Gentile mission was in God's promise from the start.

insights.title: Cursed on a tree
insights.body: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, for cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree (3:13). The shameful cross is where he bore the curse.

insights.title: The guardian
insights.body: The law was our tutor, paidagōgos, to bring us to Christ (3:24). This was a household slave who escorted a child to school and kept him in line, until he came of age.

insights.title: All one in Christ
insights.body: There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus (3:28). A Jewish morning prayer thanked God for not making one a Gentile, a slave or a woman; Paul's line overturns every one.

insights.title: Adding to grace
insights.body: The Galatians began with the Spirit but tried to finish by their own effort (3:3). Where are you trying to earn what God has already given?

4.summary: Paul explains that before Christ we were like underage heirs no better than slaves, but God sent his Son to redeem us and his Spirit to make us cry Abba; he appeals to the Galatians' early love for him and uses the story of Hagar and Sarah as an allegory of slavery and freedom.
4.lookfor: Notice the phrase "the fullness of the time," Paul's personal appeal, and the two women in the allegory.

names.name: Hagar
names.gloss: Sarah's Egyptian slave, mother of Ishmael.

names.name: Sinai
names.gloss: The mountain where the law was given.

insights.title: The heir as a child
insights.body: An heir under age is no different from a slave, under guardians until the date his father set (4:1-2). Roman fathers fixed the age when sons took full rights.

insights.title: The fullness of time
insights.body: When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law (4:4-5). The Son became what we were so we could become what he is.

insights.title: Abba
insights.body: God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father! (4:6). Abba is Aramaic, the intimate word Jesus used in Gethsemane.

insights.title: Paul's illness
insights.body: Paul first preached to them because of a weakness of the flesh, and they received him as an angel of God; they would have torn out their own eyes for him (4:13-15). Perhaps his illness affected his eyes.

insights.title: Labor pains
insights.body: My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you (4:19). Paul pictures himself as a mother giving birth a second time.

insights.title: Two women, two covenants
insights.body: Hagar the slave stands for Sinai and the present Jerusalem; Sarah the free woman stands for the Jerusalem above (4:24-26). Believers are children of promise, like Isaac.

insights.title: Back to slavery
insights.body: Paul asks how they could turn back to weak and miserable principles after knowing God (4:9). What old patterns do you keep drifting back to?

5.summary: Paul urges the Galatians to stand firm in the freedom Christ gives and not be circumcised to gain righteousness, warns that freedom is not license but a call to serve in love, and contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit.
5.lookfor: Notice how Paul defines freedom, and the two contrasting lists.

insights.title: For freedom
insights.body: Stand firm in the freedom with which Christ has made us free, and don't be entangled again with a yoke of bondage (5:1). Freedom is the theme of the last two chapters.

insights.title: Fallen from grace
insights.body: If you seek to be justified by law, you've been cut off from Christ and have fallen away from grace (5:4). Falling from grace here means trying to earn what grace gives.

insights.title: Faith working through love
insights.body: In Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, but faith working through love (5:6). Real faith expresses itself in love.

insights.title: Paul's sharpest line
insights.body: Paul wishes those who unsettle them would go further and castrate themselves (5:12). Shocking, and deliberate: if cutting saves, why stop there? In Galatia, priests of Cybele did exactly that.

insights.title: Fruit, not fruits
insights.body: The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control (5:22-23). Fruit is singular: one harvest with nine flavors, grown, not manufactured.

insights.title: Love fulfills the law
insights.body: The whole law is fulfilled in one word: love your neighbor as yourself (5:14). Freedom from the law doesn't mean lawlessness; love does what the law aimed at.

insights.title: Keeping in step
insights.body: If we live by the Spirit, let's also walk in step with the Spirit (5:25). Which fruit of the Spirit is growing slowest in you?

6.summary: Paul urges gentle restoration of those caught in sin, bearing one another's burdens, sowing to the Spirit and doing good to all; writing in large letters by his own hand, he says the only thing to boast in is the cross, by which he bears the marks of Jesus.
6.lookfor: Notice the balance of bearing others' burdens and carrying your own load, and Paul's handwritten closing.

names.name: Israel
names.gloss: Here the Israel of God, the people of God made new in Christ.

insights.title: Restore gently
insights.body: If someone is caught in a fault, you who are spiritual restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, watching yourself (6:1). Restore is the word for mending nets.

insights.title: Burdens and loads
insights.body: Bear one another's burdens (6:2), but each will carry his own load (6:5). The first word means a crushing weight; the second a soldier's pack. Help with the overwhelming, own your own responsibility.

insights.title: Sowing and reaping
insights.body: Whatever a person sows, that will they also reap (6:7). Sow to the flesh and reap corruption; sow to the Spirit and reap eternal life.

insights.title: Large letters
insights.body: See with what large letters I write to you with my own hand (6:11). Paul dictated to a scribe and added a closing in his own hand to authenticate it; large letters may reflect poor eyesight or emphasis.

insights.title: Boasting in the cross
insights.body: The rival teachers wanted to boast in the Galatians' circumcision; Paul will boast only in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ (6:14). What matters is a new creation (6:15).

insights.title: The marks of Jesus
insights.body: I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body (6:17). Slaves and devotees were branded with their owner's or god's mark; Paul's scars from beatings and stoning show whose he is.

insights.title: Don't grow weary
insights.body: Let's not grow weary in doing good, for in due season we will reap if we don't give up (6:9). Where are you tired of doing good?

intro.who: Paul wrote it to the churches of Galatia in central Asia Minor, probably those he founded on his first journey (Acts 13–14). He wrote the end in his own large handwriting (6:11).
intro.when: About AD 48–55. If written before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15, it may be Paul's earliest letter.
intro.why: Teachers had arrived insisting Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul writes urgently and angrily to defend the gospel of grace: people are made right with God by faith in Christ, not by works of the law, and are free in the Spirit.
